reasoning_details.text:
I'm working out the fixed overhead for an S-band specialist by looking at the slope between data points — roughly 7-8 TB/s throughput with about 3.2 µs of fixed cost. I'm trying to break that fixed cost down into components like launch overhead, ramp-up time, and initial DRAM latency.

For the smallest workload, I'm mapping out CTA scheduling across SMs and realizing a key insight: since all CTAs read-then-write in lockstep within one wave, the read and write phases barely overlap, essentially serializing into distinct read-drain and write-drain phases rather than pipelining together.

But I'm realizing bandwidth is shared between reads and writes regardless, so total bytes at 8TB/s gives the same time either way—serialization doesn't actually cost extra bandwidth time, just incurs latency once. Stores going to L2 with evict_last should complete quickly too, so the tail should be small.

That leaves the mystery of where the extra microseconds come from—maybe the earlier zero-fill left dirty L2 lines that get evicted and written back as our kernel allocates new lines, effectively doubling the DRAM traffic from both our reads and writes triggering write-backs.

This checks out against the larger size data too: at 805 MB, the measured bandwidth comes out near nominal, since for big sizes the dirty flush lines only get evicted once and the extra write-back cost amortizes away, whereas for small sizes it dominates since the flush write-back is comparable in size to the actual workload.

I'm now wondering whether we can avoid allocating L2 lines on reads with some no-allocate hint, but that's probably not feasible since all DRAM traffic routes through L2 anyway, and full-line stores don't need a read-before-write since L2 is write-back. The remaining question is whether the dirty flush write-back sits on the critical path through the memory controller.

Turning to fixed-cost reduction at the kernel level, I'm considering launch configuration tradeoffs — fewer, larger CTAs versus more smaller ones, and whether CTA dispatch throughput per SM/GPC becomes the bottleneck for a grid of hundreds of CTAs, or whether having each thread issue multiple loads per iteration could help amortize overhead.

I'm also wondering whether the GPU's block scheduler distributes CTAs truly round-robin across all SMs or could instead pack them onto a subset of SMs first, potentially leaving many SMs idle — which would be a major factor in explaining the observed performance if true.

I should also think about per-SM bandwidth limits: each SM handling roughly 42.5 KB reads and writes against an L1 throughput that would take around 0.44 µs, which isn't dominant but adds up, especially if load distribution across SMs is uneven. I'm starting to suspect the real bottleneck may actually be DRAM latency under contention rather than any single one of these factors.

Looking at the burst pattern, 6.3 MB of requests hits queueing limits at the DRAM. If I interleave reads and writes so some CTAs finish early and start writing while others are still loading, the DRAM bus is still shared, so I'd expect roughly 1.68 µs total bus time for both read and write drains combined — unless the writes are cached with evict_last and land in L2 instead of going straight to DRAM, since 6.3MB easily fits within the 126MB L2. That would mean writes ride on the much faster L2 bandwidth rather than DRAM bandwidth.

But those L2-resident writes cause evictions of dirty lines when the cache needs space, pushing writeback traffic to DRAM anyway — so DRAM ends up seeing the 6.3MB of reads plus around 12.6MB of write-back traffic, totaling near 19MB, which at 8TB/s comes to about 2.4µs, plus roughly 1µs latency and 0.5µs launch overhead gets me close to 4µs, matching the observed 4.8µs figure. This makes me wonder if I can avoid allocating input reads in L2 at all, perhaps using an evict-first policy so clean input lines get evicted ahead of the dirty output lines, freeing space for outputs without triggering extra write-backs.

But that exact "evict-first on loads" idea for S was already tried and measured — the rented B200 run showed S at 5.4 vs the parent's 5.6, so it's already accounted for and not a new direction. I need to look elsewhere within the S specialist: maybe reshaping the grid to exactly 148×k CTAs with balanced work and larger per-thread loads, issuing all loads upfront to reduce dispatch overhead, though row counts don't divide evenly by 148 so I'd need a persistent-style assignment with a tail loop to stay correct across all S shapes.

Checking row counts for the S-band token sizes, and recalling that the 2-rows-per-thread and Q/K-pair-per-thread variants were already tested across all sizes with S scores around 5.9 and 5.5. I'm also considering whether I could influence CTA-to-SM placement via dynamic work-stealing with an atomic counter that self-resets when the last CTA finishes, but that introduces cross-call state which risks correctness and isn't really viable here.

Going through other angles: thread block clusters don't help, instruction count isn't the bottleneck, and L2 prefetching for the whole input tile at kernel start is essentially the already-proposed l2pf variant. I'm wondering whether launch overhead scales with CTA/register size, and whether store instructions with eviction hints could reduce DRAM write-back pressure for the S band outputs that stay resident in L2 — though that doesn't seem to pan out either. Now I'm thinking about whether marking input reads to avoid L2 allocation entirely might help.

Since all NVIDIA memory traffic routes through L2 there's no true bypass, but streaming load hints like .lu behave like evict-first, and discarding L2 lines for our own input data after reading looks tempting — except that's only safe if those lines aren't dirty. Since the harness's input copy step writes fresh data into the pool right before our kernel runs, those lines are dirty in L2, so discarding them would lose data rather than just evict cleanly.

That rules out the discard trick entirely since we don't own write access to the input tensor and corrupting it is out of bounds. So I'm back to structural levers — CTA count, thread count, bytes per thread — and comparing against the physical lower bound: looking at how the reference CAKE kernel scales (2.1MB in 2.53µs, 8.4MB in 3.49µs, 25.2MB in 6.37µs) against our own numbers to see where the real bottleneck sits.

Interpolating CAKE's slope suggests at 12.6MB we should land near 4.2µs, but we're at 4.8µs — roughly 0.6µs of extra cost somewhere at that smaller size, even though our slope at larger sizes is actually better than CAKE's. I'm suspecting this comes down to CTA imbalance: 768 CTAs across 148 SMs splits unevenly, leaving some SMs with 6 CTAs and others with 5, which could explain the extra latency at that specific size.

Working through the per-SM data movement: each SM handling 6 CTAs needs roughly 96 KB of combined reads and writes, which at 96 GB/s takes about 1 µs. Breaking it down by direction, reads alone at 64 B/clk take around 750 clocks (0.5 µs), so the read/write balance still matters but isn't the dominant constraint.

Now I'm thinking about how to design a well-balanced grid: ideally 148×k CTAs where rows are split as evenly as possible across SMs, so each SM gets nearly identical work. With 12,288 total rows (Q+K combined), that comes out to about 83 rows per SM.

I'm considering a flat, strided assignment of rows to half-warps across CTAs so that neighboring half-warps read contiguous rows, keeping memory access coalesced while balancing load evenly.

Actually with strided half-warp assignment the imbalance is worse than I thought — it concentrates extra rows into the first set of CTAs rather than spreading them evenly, giving a 1.5× load imbalance between busiest and least-busy CTA. A better approach is to split rows into contiguous near-equal chunks per CTA (83 or 84 rows each), then within each CTA stride the half-warps across that chunk.

But this assumes the CTAs actually land one-per-SM on the hardware scheduler, which isn't guaranteed — if the scheduler packs multiple CTAs onto fewer SMs instead of distributing breadth-first, the balance I'm computing is moot regardless of how I partition rows.

I'm realizing register pressure naturally works in my favor: if each thread needs around 60 registers to hold its data, then with 1024 threads per block that's close to filling the entire register file, which would force exactly one CTA per SM and guarantee spread across all SMs without extra tricks.

I'm considering whether weight loads could be shared across rows when the stride between them is a multiple of 48, which would cut down redundant fetches. Testing a design with 64 half-warps per CTA and roughly 83 rows, so most half-warps handle one row and a fraction handle two — this keeps per-SM balance fine since the workload is mostly memory-bound anyway.

For the larger S band with ~56,256 rows across SMs, I calculate each thread would need to process around 6 rows, which risks register spills given the 1024-thread, 64-register budget. I'm now trying to template the kernel on rows-per-thread, keeping launch bounds fixed at 1024 threads per CTA, with each CTA assigned a contiguous row chunk.

I'm weighing whether loading weights after the reduction is worth the added L2 latency, and considering whether 1024-thread CTAs with RPT 6 would spill registers given the 96-register footprint, which pushes me to reconsider how weight rows map across half-warps for the 586-token case.

If I make the chunk base a multiple of 48, each half-warp can share a single weight head across its rows, so I'm thinking of organizing CTAs into 48 half-warps per row-group and splitting the combined Q/K token range evenly across CTAs, balanced to within one token.

That stride-48 assignment lets each half-warp handle rows sharing the same head, loading weights once. But I need to handle the Q/K boundary carefully—since weight tensors differ between Q and K, I should avoid chunks straddling that boundary by splitting CTAs cleanly between Q-only and K-only assignments.

Running the numbers for different sequence lengths: with R=6144 and NB=148, I get 74 CTAs per stream and chunks around 83-84 rows, needing RPT=2 per half-warp. For 256 tokens (R=12288), chunks of 166 rows need RPT=4. For 131 tokens, chunks of 85 rows still fit RPT=2, and for 586 tokens, chunks of 380 rows require RPT=8.

Checking register pressure for RPT=8: roughly 82 registers per thread across 768 threads comes to about 63K total, which just fits one CTA per SM given the 85-register ceiling from launch bounds. But register allocation rounds to multiples of 8, so 80 regs might be too tight and risk spilling -- I'm considering whether a smaller NB like 296 with RPT=4 could let two CTAs share an SM instead, trading occupancy against per-thread register budget.

I'm now questioning whether weight sharing across rows is even necessary, since weights are only 48KB total and mostly hit in L1 cache anyway, making the extra registers for reuse possibly not worth it compared to just loading 16 regs per row directly.

I'm not confident launch timing alone explains it, but the fixed placement of 148 CTAs forcing one-per-SM guarantees even die usage, which seems like a stronger robustness factor. There's also the question of whether the 3.2 µs includes final memory flush and store visibility at kernel end, plus how DRAM queuing behaves under the full 6.3 MB burst.

Thinking through the full memory traffic: reads evict dirty lines causing write-backs during the read phase too, and the output writes themselves trigger more evictions, so total DRAM traffic could be around 6.3 MB reads plus roughly double that in write-backs, pushing total time closer to 4 µs. One way to cut this down would be prioritizing eviction of input lines so output writes replace clean lines instead of dirty ones, avoiding the extra flush traffic.

After zero-fill, L2 holds mostly dirty lines, so if the harness copies inputs before flushing, that should be fine since the flush evicts them anyway. I'm tempted to combine my new grid design with evict_first loads, but the task wants the change isolated — combining would confound results from the S specialist, so I should keep loads at default policy and stores as evict_last like the parent, varying only the grid and work distribution to isolate the actual change being tested.

I'm also wondering whether this grid redesign is really the best lever for cutting the measured ~1 µs, versus something like TLB warmth effects from the flush buffer touching unrelated pages, or how CUPTI's timing window interacts with the end of the zero-fill kernel and the start of ours.

Given typical B200 empty-kernel overhead and DRAM round-trip costs, I'm estimating the fixed cost breaks down into roughly half a microsecond for launch/teardown, about a microsecond for the first load's DRAM latency, another half to one microsecond from dirty-L2 writeback contention, and a few tenths from imbalance or tail effects. I'll settle on the balanced one-CTA-per-SM design with stride-48 weight reuse, though I still want to weigh two CTAs per SM as an alternative.

With 148 total blocks split 74/74 between Q and K streams, each SM handles one stream's chunk, which seems workable. A single 768-thread CTA per SM gives 24 warps, and each thread issues its loads plus one weight load—manageable memory footprint even for the smallest case, though stores get predicated so half-warps with fewer rows sit idle. My main worry is that with register usage low enough to fit two CTAs per SM, the scheduler could pack two CTAs onto one SM and leave others empty, which would break the balanced design.

The CTA scheduler generally distributes round-robin across SMs, so 148 CTAs should map one-to-one onto 148 SMs, but to guarantee this I'd need to either force shared memory usage high enough to cap occupancy at 1 CTA/SM, or push register usage above 32 per thread with 1024 threads so that 2 CTAs can't fit (65536 register limit). The shared-memory approach risks changing the carve-out configuration at launch time, which could add reconfiguration overhead, while the register-pressure approach seems safer but shifts the half-warp stride from 64 to 48, which I need to account for.

That remark was actually about grid-size-dependent SM filling order, not relevant since 148 CTAs fill all SMs anyway. I'm thinking I should just use __launch_bounds__(768, 1) and consider adding minimal static shared memory, though exceeding 114 KB would force one block per SM and require the dynamic opt-in path.

48KB static max only gives 4 CTAs, so I'd need dynamic smem with cudaFuncSetAttribute at init, though the L1/shared carve-out reconfiguration cost at kernel boundaries is uncertain. Forcing higher register usage via launch bounds doesn't give fine control, so that's not a reliable lever either. A more robust approach might avoid relying on placement heuristics altogether.

Using smid to pick which chunk a CTA processes doesn't help since two CTAs could still land on the same SM and double its workload, and there's no guarantee of exactly one CTA per SM. I'll just go with the breadth-first assumption and actually test it, since I noticed the local GPU is a B200 — so I can get real rented-B200 timings for S directly rather than guessing, and the parent's S number was 5.6 on rented hardware. I'm also checking whether an RPT-variant fits for a 586-token chunk, since 48 half-warps at RPT 8 pushes register overhead past the 80 limit for 768 threads, so I'm considering NB=296 instead.

Trying 2 CTAs per SM with RPT=4 pushes register usage too high to fit (86K vs 64K budget), and switching to 384 threads creates alternating weight-row complications that add more register pressure. Falling back to stride-48 with 768 threads and RPT=4 still exceeds the per-thread register ceiling once weights are included, so it looks like spilling is unavoidable unless I load weights lazily from L1 after the reduction instead of keeping them all in registers.

Maybe I should just let 586 fall through to the parent kernel since it already covers B·S ≤ 600, narrowing the specialist kernel to only 4 workloads. I'll make the kernel generic over RPT and CTA count via templates, picking per-workload configs — for tokens 128/131 I'll use NB=148, RPT=2 with 768 threads, and for 256 I'm working out NB=148 with RPT=4 and checking the resulting register count.

For the 586 case, bumping RPT to 8 risks too many registers, so I'm considering NB=296 with 2 CTAs per SM and smaller RPT/thread counts instead, or just reloading weights per row and relying on L1 caching rather than sharing weights explicitly across a stride pattern.

1024-thread CTAs would give 64 half-warps per stride, but 64 mod 48 cycles heads across 3 values, so that's messier. I'll default 586 to the parent unless the RPT=8 specialist compiles without spilling — the gain is small, maybe 5% off the fixed cost, roughly +0.0015 score, worth a quick check but not a priority. There might also be a two-phase alternative for large RPT worth exploring.

Per-SM memory layout probably doesn't matter much since DRAM channel interleaving spreads addresses finely regardless of contiguous vs interleaved chunking. For the Q/K split with NB=148, both halves get equal CTA counts and equal work, so die placement shouldn't affect balance even if the scheduler assigns ids in blocks rather than round-robin.

I'm sketching the kernel signature for the fused QK RMSNorm kernel, computing which CTA handles Q vs K based on block index, then deriving the balanced row chunk boundaries and thread-to-head mapping.

I realize since predicated rows depend on h which is shared across 16 lanes but differs between half-warps in the same warp, I need to use `__shfl_xor_sync` carefully to avoid divergence issues within the shuffle reduction.

Now I'm working out the host-side dispatch logic: computing tokens and row counts, then picking the smallest RPT template (from {1,2,3,4,6,8}) that covers the needed chunk size per half-warp, checking a few example token counts like 128, 256, and 586 to confirm the formula holds generically.

I'm setting a threshold for when to fall back to the parent kernel (tokens > 600 or rpt_needed > 8), and now checking register usage and launch bounds for the RPT=8 variant to make sure it compiles cleanly without spilling.

Let me just test the compile and see what happens.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm puzzling over why fewer warps per SM performs worse here — more rows per thread seems to cause serialization despite similar total bytes in flight, with the 37% slowdown at RPT 8 suggesting something about how stride-48 rows map across half-warps and per-SM throughput limits.

I'm wondering if it's the store phase bottlenecking per-SM throughput, or register pressure (80 regs) preventing multiple CTAs per SM the way lower-register configs allow. The real issue might be DRAM locality: with my mapping, all SMs simultaneously read from widely separated large contiguous chunks, which could create L2 slice or channel conflicts, whereas the parent's approach spreads smaller contiguous reads across SMs more evenly — suggesting more CTAs with more total threads is the better direction.

I try an alternate interleaved mapping where consecutive CTAs handle strided tokens with adjacent row offsets for better locality, but token-granularity balancing gets messy when it doesn't divide evenly across 148 CTAs. Given the results, I suspect the dominant cost is per-thread serial latency tied to rows-per-thread, so I consider shrinking CTA size further (64 threads, 4 rows) to push CTA count up to 3072, though that bumps against the 32 CTAs/SM limit.

That interleaving creates imbalance but reveals a locality effect, though the one-CTA-per-SM constraint remains a problem. I'm wondering if the real bottleneck is actually write-back of dirty L2 lines during the store phase rather than load balancing, which might explain why the EF-load variant performs slightly better — though stores inherently require writing those lines regardless.

Pre-fetching inputs from L2 wouldn't help since they're cold anyway. Trying a quarter-warp-per-row split with fewer, heavier-loaded threads performs worse, while spreading to full 32 lanes with lighter loads per thread gives a modest gain — suggesting the degradation with repeated loads may come from predicated branches preventing the compiler from hoisting loads, even though they're non-blocking and issued back-to-back within each block.

Now I'm looking at CTA occupancy: register pressure limits whether 1 or 2 CTAs fit per SM, and the configurations guaranteeing only a single CTA per SM seem to pay a real performance cost. With load issue throughput being trivial relative to warp count, the real bottleneck might be DRAM locality — each SM streams its own contiguous region of memory, and with many concurrent streams hitting different addresses, that could be where the slowdown originates.

Thinking about B200's address interleaving across channels, the parent's dense contiguous access spreads naturally across channels, but my 148 separate 83KB regions might not spread as evenly depending on where the interleave hashing collides. Testing an interleaved token mapping directly would help isolate whether that's the real cause.

Switching to token-granular striding for locality, computing rows-per-tile from ceil(tokens/nb_half) across different token counts to keep templates consistent.

reasoning_details.text:
I notice something odd at 256 tokens: the parent stays at 5.6 while all my variants jump to 6.0+, but the reference stays steady. With 1536 CTAs of 256 tokens, that's 10.4 per SM, exceeding 8 resident, so the parent actually runs a second partial wave and still wins — suggesting the extra wave isn't the bottleneck I assumed.

Maybe what matters is overlap between DRAM reads and write-backs across waves: single-wave designs do all reads then all writes serially, while two waves let wave 2's loads overlap wave 1's stores. If that's the real driver, software-pipelined overlap between CTAs is the key benefit, and I could test it by deliberately capping resident CTAs per SM (via launch bounds or shared memory) to force multiple waves even at small token counts, like restricting to 4 CTAs/SM for ROWS 16 so 768 CTAs form 1.3 waves instead of one.

But looking at the actual timing data, this wave-count theory doesn't hold up cleanly — ROWS4 and ROWS48 both produced multiple waves yet still ran slower than the parent, so wave count alone isn't the deciding factor. With limited GPU calls remaining, the parent configuration still looks like a solid local optimum, and the more promising lead is the persistent, software-pipelined approach that outperformed us at the 25MB size by loading the next tile while storing the current one for continuous overlap.

None of the probes tested actually beat the baseline — ROWS8 ties exactly at 0% for 131/586. I'm considering a couple more long-shot ideas: reordering the CTA grid to interleave Q and K tiles instead of grouping them, though that seems unlikely to matter, and trying the texture-cache load path via `ld.global.nc` since eviction hints on stores probably won't help since the S band output stays in L2 regardless.

One more angle is prefetching the next wave's tile into L2 at kernel start, but that's basically the same as an earlier L2-prefetch idea I already considered for a different band. A more general version — each CTA prefetching the tile that the CTA offset by the resident capacity will need — would only actually trigger benefit for multi-wave cases like 256 tokens or 586, since single-wave sizes wouldn't see any effect.

Right now, second-wave CTAs don't start fetching from DRAM until a first-wave CTA retires, which adds roughly a microsecond of latency to the critical path; prefetching during wave 1 should shave off maybe half a microsecond to a microsecond on those two cases. I'm weighing whether to issue the prefetch per-cache-line across many threads or use a single bulk prefetch instruction from one thread to cover the whole 8 KB tile.

With resident occupancy at 8 CTAs per SM (148 total), I'm figuring out the right target tile offset for prefetching ahead — one tile-width for the smaller workload, possibly two tiles ahead for the larger one if enough CTAs exist. Since the prefetched lines land in L2 and total DRAM bytes moved stays the same either way, this shouldn't hurt bandwidth, it just removes the latency bubble.

If prefetch is issued right as wave-1 CTAs launch, essentially all the data gets requested within the first microsecond, keeping DRAM continuously busy without hurting correctness. I want to bound the prefetch to valid tensor addresses only and restrict this change to the small-token dispatch path (≤600 tokens) to isolate its effect, even though the medium band with many waves could benefit similarly — sticking to S-only for now per the isolation requirement. Using the default eviction policy, the wave-2 CTA's demand load should then hit L2 at roughly 0.3-0.5 µs instead of the ~1 µs DRAM round trip, so now I need to work out the implementation details.

I'm having thread 0 of each CTA compute the address of a tile several waves ahead and issue an async bulk prefetch into L2, choosing lookahead offsets based on how many waves exist for each token-count case (e.g. 1184 and 2368 tiles ahead for 586 tokens, 1184 for 256), and placing this prefetch after the CTA's own loads so it doesn't delay critical work. I'm now noticing an issue: since each wave's CTAs also prefetch ahead by the same offset, a wave-2 CTA ends up prefetching the same tile that a wave-1 CTA already prefetched two offsets ago, causing redundant prefetch requests.

reasoning_details.text:
Prefetching actually hurt 586 by 9%, which suggests DRAM bandwidth is already the bottleneck there rather than latency bubbles — extra early requests just add congestion, with effective traffic exceeding nominal due to dirty write-backs. That points toward the EF-loads mechanism of reducing write-back traffic, though I can't reproduce that here.

Working through the allocation footprint: inputs plus outputs totals 12.6 MB, so write-back and reads sum to 18.9 MB naively, but evict-first ordering could cut that to 12.6 MB if inputs get evicted before flush lines — yet the rented r6 test only showed a 4% gain at S, so maybe write-backs happen lazily outside the measurement window. Writing outputs directly into the same L2 lines isn't feasible either.

With only two GPU calls left and everything tested so far worse or equal to baseline, I need to pick one real candidate to submit — since the portal compresses differences at S, I should try one more genuinely distinct mechanism rather than a variant that's already been shown equivalent.

I'm considering pairing Q and K loads within the same CTA, but that's already been tried as r6-qkpair. Splitting each CTA's tile into two sequential halves is essentially RPT=2, which performed worse. The prefetch-hurts-performance result is puzzling since L2 is 126 MB and shouldn't be evicting prefetched data, and limiting concurrency to reduce DRAM congestion doesn't fit since the parent's 2-wave config already beat single-wave configs at 256 tokens. Given all this, my best remaining idea is testing an interleaved Q/K CTA ordering so each wave touches both streams, or trying L1::no_allocate on the loads — though both feel like low-probability wins at this point.

Reads issued first still interleave with triggered write-backs anyway, so that angle doesn't help. With only two calls left and low confidence in other variants, I'll try one more: interleaving Q and K CTA order with reversed grid index, though I don't expect much from it.

I'm weighing whether to try throttling resident CTAs via shared memory sizing instead -- adjusting dynamic smem to control CTAs per SM -- but the wave math doesn't favor it much either. At this point I need to settle on which tested candidate to actually submit, since no single configuration wins across all sizes.

Comparing projected scores: the prefetch variant and the ROWS4/8 variant both land below parent, roughly equally. The prefetch version clearly regresses at 586, while ROWS4/8 is neutral at 131/586 but worse at 128/256, and ROWS48/24 is neutral at 128 but gains at 586 and 256. I'm tempted to stitch together a dispatcher that picks ROWS8 for the 131-600 range and falls back to parent elsewhere, though that would require re-validating the combined code.

Since I only have two calls left, I'll test ROWS8 across all tokens ≤600 as a clean S-specialist using 128-thread CTAs, 16 per SM, since that configuration hasn't been measured yet at 128/256. It's a low-risk way to probe CTA-size sensitivity.
